title: Surface Drift: token guardrails and interactive component adaptors for deep-dark console themes
creator: Ava Chen
description:
Problem: As we expand brand variants and support deeper dark themes, component visuals are drifting from intended contrast and spacing — particularly on compact interactive elements (compact buttons, condensed tables, and micro charts). This ticket establishes explicit token guardrails and per-component adaptor rules so brand accents and deep-dark fallbacks do not cause surface drift or hit accessibility failures.

Scope:
- Define 'token guardrails' (min/max contrast deltas) for surface and ink tokens across density modes.
- Produce per-component adaptor rules for buttons, table rows, and chart strokes so brand accents can be applied without breaking contrast or layout.
- Provide a recommended mapping file (human-readable) for runtime/platform engineers to implement in the theme layer.
- Validate through design QA and a small set of automated color-contrast checks integrated with the Console design-test harness.

Non-goals: full token rename or wholesale semantic token migration (handled in separate migration epic). This is a tactical, backwards-compatible adaptor layer to be upstreamed into runtime-1.18 and console-2025.03.
acceptance_criteria: A compact button token map exists showing primary/secondary/ghost variants with deep-dark fallback values that meet WCAG AA for normal text (4.5:1) and 3:1 for UI components where applicable
Per-component adaptors for tables and charts documented with examples and before/after screenshots (desktop and compact density)
Design QA checklist created and linked; two sample dashboards tested with the new mappings and no regressions on contrast or spacing
Token mapping doc approved by design lead and sign-off from the runtime owner (ENG) for integration
proposed_token_map:
# Proposed human-readable adaptor map (subset)
surface-0 -> surface-100  (light) | dark-fallback: surface-800
surface-50 -> surface-200   | dark-fallback: surface-780
surface-100 -> surface-250  | dark-fallback: surface-760
ink-100 -> ink-300 (buttons primary text) | in deep-dark replace with ink-100-on-accent when accent is present
accent-primary -> accent-primary (brand) | when contrast<3.5 on surface fallback to accent-muted
button-padding-compact -> 6px 8px | ensures min hit area preserved
table-row-separator -> 1px solid surface-300 | deep-dark fallback surface-700
chart-stroke-compact -> stroke-width: 1.5px; color: accent-primary or accent-muted (if contrast fails)

Notes: This is intentionally prescriptive (not just semantic) so engineers can implement an adaptor layer that computes fallback values when brand accents reduce contrast. The runtime should expose a small set of hooks: computeFallback(tokenName, brandColor, density).
technical_notes: Trade-offs discussed: stronger guardrails reduce brand expressiveness; we bias to reliability for console-critical UI (tables, buttons) and allow looser rules for marketing components
Implementation suggestion: add adaptor layer between theme resolution and component render; keep semantic tokens unchanged and compute effective token at runtime
Runtime owners requested a minimal API: { tokenName, brandColorHex, density, mode } -> resolvedTokenHex; provide unit tests that assert contrast ratios
We will follow up with a small ENG spike (1 week) to prototype the adaptor API and run against ten sample brand colors
